title: Frequency map
summary: Count values with a Map and return the most frequent one deterministically.

scenario.briefing: The campus analytics desk needs the most frequent value in a list. Ties must resolve to the lexicographically smallest value so reports are deterministic.

objectives.description: Check understanding through the remaining explanation and transfer evidence.

hints: Create a Map from value to count.
Loop over values and increment the stored count.
Track the best value and break ties with localeCompare or <.
For each value, update its count; if count is higher, or equal and the value sorts earlier, replace the best.

misconceptions.description: Using a plain object for arbitrary key values.
misconceptions.feedback: A Map handles any key type without prototype collisions and preserves clear counting semantics.

misconceptions.description: Returning whichever value happens to be seen first on a tie.
misconceptions.testDescription: Tie between three values picks the smallest.
misconceptions.feedback: Input order should not silently decide a tie. Use the documented lexical rule.

misconceptions.description: Believing a frequency map makes pairwise comparison linear.
misconceptions.feedback: One map lookup is constant, but comparing every pair still needs n times n comparisons.

misconceptions.description: Believing a Map guarantees sorted iteration.
misconceptions.feedback: A Map preserves insertion order for iteration in JavaScript, not sorted key order.

sections.title: Count with a hash map
sections.body: A Map stores key-value pairs. Counting assigns each distinct value a number, giving expected O(1) lookup per element and O(n) total work. This is faster than comparing every pair.

sections.title: Determinism is part of correctness
sections.body: When several values share the highest count, a report needs a rule. Choosing the lexicographically smallest makes output reproducible regardless of input order or language implementation details.

vocabulary.definition: A key-value structure with fast lookup.
How many times a value occurs.
Producing the same result for the same input.

hints: Count each distinct value before choosing a winner.

steps.title: Why a Map?
steps.prompt: Counting n values with a Map takes expected O(n) work. What would comparing every pair cost?

quiz.explanation: Comparing each element with every other is quadratic. A frequency map avoids the repeated scan.

hints: Each of n elements can compare with up to n others.
The growth is n times n.

steps.title: Hash map trade-offs

statements.label: A Map gives expected constant-time lookup.
A frequency map uses additional memory proportional to distinct values.
A Map guarantees sorted key order.
Tie-breaking must be explicit for deterministic output.

steps.explanation: Hash maps trade memory for fast lookup. They do not provide sorted iteration.
hints: A hash map trades memory for lookup speed.
Keys are not stored in sorted order.
Tie-breaking is a correctness rule, not an implementation detail.
Select expected constant lookup, extra memory, and explicit ties; reject sorted key order.
